1.c4 Nf6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight towards the centre, where it controls d5 and e4, and keeps e4, g3 and d4 all available. White decides later between taking the centre, a fianchetto set-up and a flexible waiting game, and keeps more options against Black's set-up. The cost is that the centre stays unoccupied for now: Black can contest it at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight, watches d4 and e5 and leaves the choice between d4, g3 and Nc3 open until Black's set-up is clear. White can still go for a Queen's pawn game with d4 or for a flexible fianchetto set-up. The move commits little, though it gives Black a free choice of defensive scheme.

1.c4 Nf6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn, and the game becomes a queen's pawn opening. White gets the c4-d4 pawn pair and extra space, but the pawns become targets, and White must be ready for whichever defence Black picks.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2, which bears on d5 and along the long diagonal towards b7, and keeps the knights' development and d4 in reserve. White aims for a flexible fianchetto set-up. The cost is that the centre stays unoccupied, and Black can challenge the c4-pawn at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports d4, a solid set-up that commits the e-pawn before Black's set-up is known. It is slow: Black can take space at once and develop freely.

1.c4 Nf6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2, which bears on e5 and the long diagonal, and supports the c4-pawn. It is sound but slow: the centre stays unoccupied, and Black can claim it with pawns or contest the diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.d3.strategy: Supports a later e4 and opens the c1-bishop. It is sound but modest: d4 would now cost an extra tempo, so Black can take the centre at once and develop freely.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qc2.strategy: Backs the c4-pawn and prepares e4, but develops no minor piece and leaves the queen where ...Nc6 followed by ...Nb4 can hit it with tempo. Black takes the centre at once while White is still unready.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qb3.strategy: Eyes b7 and defends the c4-pawn, but the c8-bishop already covers b7 and no minor piece is developed. ...Nc6 followed by ...Na5 then hits the queen and the c4-pawn with tempo, and Black takes the centre while White rearranges.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Qa4.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and pins the d7-pawn for a moment, but threatens nothing real. ...c6 breaks the pin and prepares ...d5, and Black develops freely while the queen stands on the rim.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Na3.strategy: Defends the c4-pawn and can continue to c2 or b5, but on a3 the knight controls no central square. Black takes the centre in the meantime.

1.c4 Nf6 2.Nh3.strategy: Develops the knight on the rim on its way to f4 and leaves the centre alone. Once Black's d-pawn has moved, ...Bxh3 can double White's h-pawns, and f3 was the natural square for the knight.

1.c4 Nf6 2.a3.strategy: Takes b4 from Black's pieces and prepares b4, but spends a tempo without developing anything or touching the centre. Black takes space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.a4.strategy: Gains a little queenside space but develops nothing and gives up the b4-square for good, where a black knight or bishop can settle. Black takes the centre in the meantime.

1.c4 Nf6 2.b4.name: English Orangutan
1.c4 Nf6 2.b4.strategy: Advances the b-pawn where nothing defends it: after ...e6 or ...e5 the f8-bishop attacks it, and White must spend another tempo saving it or give it up. Development lags while Black takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.f3.strategy: Prepares e4 but takes f3 from the knight, weakens the e1-h4 diagonal and develops nothing. Black develops freely and takes the centre at once.

1.c4 Nf6 2.f4.name: Bird Opening: Mujannah
1.c4 Nf6 2.f4.strategy: Grabs kingside space and controls e5, but opens the e1-h4 diagonal to the king and develops nothing. Black can simply develop and take the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.h3.strategy: Stops ...Ng4 and ...Bg4 but is a slow waiting move that develops nothing. Black takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on the edge of the board, weakens the g3-square, develops no piece and does nothing for the centre. Black takes space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.c5.strategy: Gains space but moves the same pawn twice and gives up control of d5. The pawn on c5 has no defender: ...e6 or ...e5 opens the f8-bishop against it and ...b6 undermines it, while White has developed nothing.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g4.strategy: Hangs a pawn: 2...Nxg4 wins it at once because nothing defends g4, and h3 only drives the knight to a good square like e5. The kingside is loosened with no lead in development in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn: Black simply wins a pawn with 2...Nxe4, and quick development does not regain it, since the knight can retreat to f6 or c5.

1.c4 Nf6.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defence
1.c4 Nf6.background: The most common reply to 1.c4; the Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings classifies its independent lines as A15 to A19.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 and commits to little else, so Black keeps a solid centre and a flexible pawn structure and decides later how to meet White's set-up. The price is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn for the time being.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's fianchetto and prepares ...Bg7 and short castling, so both sides control the centre from a distance. Black can later occupy it with pawns or challenge it with ...d5. The game stays flexible and tends to be a manoeuvring fight over the centre rather than an early clash.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with a pawn behind it, so that cxd5 can be met by ...cxd5 instead of ...Nxd5, where the knight would stand exposed to Bg2. Black gets a solid pawn structure in which the queen's bishop can still develop before ...e6. The c-pawn is committed, so a later ...c5 costs an extra tempo.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c5.strategy: Controls d4 and heads for a symmetrical pawn structure, where the fight is over d4 and over queenside expansion with b4 or ...b5. Black accepts that White is a move ahead and has to meet the coming pressure of White's fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 e5.strategy: Takes the centre at once with a pawn and reaches a reversed Sicilian, in which White has the extra tempo. The game turns on control of d5: White fights for it with the c-pawn, the fianchettoed bishop and the knight, while Black defends the centre with solid development.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 d5.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once, but after 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.Bg2 the bishop attacks the knight on d5. Black must spend a move saving the knight, so White develops with gain of time; preparing ...d5 first avoids this.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares ...e5 to take space in the centre. It is sound but less flexible than a quieter pawn move: the knight blocks the c-pawn and commits the queen's knight before Black knows White's set-up.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the diagonal of the c8-bishop, while a kingside fianchetto stays available. It is sound but modest: the pawn claims less central space than a more direct stand, so White can build up in the centre and keep a small space advantage.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop to challenge the long diagonal. It is sound, but White can expand in the centre with e4 fairly easily, and Black has less say there than after a more solid pawn move first.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but does little for the centre. It needs more moves to become useful, while White gains space in the centre unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 a6.strategy: Slow, and the ...b5 it prepares fails tactically: once the b-pawn leaves b7, the bishop on g2 hits the rook on a8, so 3.Bg2 b5 4.Bxa8 takes the rook.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 a5.strategy: A slow edge-pawn move that restrains b4 but weakens b5 and does nothing for the centre or for development, while White develops unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. White builds a space advantage without hindrance.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 h5.strategy: Heads for ...h4 against g3, but after 3.Nf3 the push ...h4 just drops a pawn to Nxh4, as the g3-pawn guards the knight. The move also weakens g5 and makes kingside castling less attractive while White develops.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ng8.strategy: Undoes Black's first move and returns the knight to its starting square, so White has made two useful moves to none and keeps a free hand in the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ng4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time without a real threat, since the king guards f2 and the rook guards h2. After 3.h3 it has to move a third time, while White develops unhindered.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nh5.strategy: Aims at g3, but the pawn is guarded by f2 and h2, so nothing is threatened. The rim knight can be harassed: 3.e4 opens the queen's diagonal to h5, and White gains time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Ne4.strategy: Moves the knight a second time to a square where no pawn supports it: 3.d3 drives it away at once, and White gains time and space while the knight looks for a safe square.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Rg8.strategy: Spends a tempo and gives up kingside castling for good, since the h8-rook has moved, without helping development or the centre. White simply develops and takes the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 b5.strategy: Gives up a pawn for little: after 3.cxb5 the long diagonal is open, so Bg2 will hit the rook on a8, and Black has to spend time on it instead of on queenside pressure in return for the pawn.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g5.strategy: Weakens f5, h5 and the future king's cover, and the pawn needs support at once: 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against it. The loosened kingside remains a lasting weakness.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 Nd5.strategy: Hangs the knight: the c4-pawn attacks d5 and nothing defends it, as the d7-pawn blocks the queen, so 3.cxd5 wins a piece for nothing.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3.strategy: The flexible developing move: it guards d4 and e5, readies castling and keeps White's central pawn plans open. Against Black's pawn on c6, White aims at a slow game of pressure down the long diagonal rather than an early fight for the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.d4.strategy: Builds a pawn centre at once. With pawns on c4 and d4 White has more space than Black, whose pawn on c6 and a coming ...d5 meet it solidly. The game becomes a fight over the structure of the centre rather than a slow build-up with pieces.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Bg2.strategy: Completes the fianchetto at once, aiming the bishop down the long diagonal at the pawn on c6 and preparing castling. The pawn on c6 blunts the bishop's diagonal, so White builds slowly with pieces and settles the centre later.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3 d5.strategy: Completes the solid pair of pawns on c6 and d5: the centre square is defended by pawn, knight and queen, and the bishop on c8 stays free to develop outside the pawn chain. Black accepts less space for a robust structure that White's coming fianchetto has to bite on.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's fianchetto: the bishop will watch the long diagonal and the king castles behind a flexible pawn structure. Black holds back the central pawn move and decides the centre later, at the cost of some space.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 c6 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: A solid but passive set-up: the pawn on e6 prepares ...d5 and guards the centre, but it shuts in the bishop on c8, which then needs time to find a good square. Black gets a sound structure and a slightly cramped game.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal, where it presses on d5 and the queenside from a safe distance behind the g3 pawn. White matches Black's set-up and keeps the centre pawns uncommitted, so the game stays flexible for a while.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, where with the bishop to come it fights for d5 and e4. White leaves open whether to build a pawn centre or play a slower game, but lets Black strike with ...d5 before the bishop is out.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to cover d4 and e5 and keeps both the bishop move and the pawn centre in reserve. White stays flexible and can still choose between a space-gaining centre and a quieter game of manoeuvre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.d4.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre before the bishop is out. Black can fianchetto in reply and play against the d4 pawn, or hit back in the centre at once; White gets the space, Black the long diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up: the bishop takes the long diagonal and the way is clear to castle. Black keeps the choice open between challenging the centre at once and building a compact position first.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 d5.strategy: Challenges the c4 pawn at once, before White's pieces are out. Black opens the centre and develops quickly, but the knight that recaptures on d5 faces the bishop on g2 and a possible e-pawn push, so the king's bishop and castling should not wait long.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's pawn and prepares to challenge d4 from the flank. Black keeps the centre closed and plays for queenside space, but spends a move on a pawn while the kingside is undeveloped, which gives White time to develop and claim the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4.strategy: Stakes a claim in the centre with a pawn and gains space. Black must decide whether to challenge that centre at once or to castle first and let White build; White's task is to turn the extra space into something lasting.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Puts a knight in the centre, where it works with the bishop on g2 against d5 and e4. White does not yet commit the d-pawn and keeps the choice between a broad pawn centre and a quiet, flexible set-up.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to cover d4 and e5 and prepares to castle. White holds back the d-pawn and keeps the choice between a pawn centre and a slower, manoeuvring game, while Black has to commit to a set-up first.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O.strategy: Tucks the king away and delays the choice of pawn structure. A flexible, solid approach: White has to commit first, and Black accepts conceding some space in return.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5.name: Grünfeld Defence: Counterthrust Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5.strategy: Strikes at once and attacks the c4 pawn before White's pieces are out. White chooses between releasing the tension and developing, and Black answers either with active piece play against the pawn centre instead of defending it passively.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and c5 with the pawn and opens the c8-bishop, a compact structure that postpones all decisions. Sound, but it leaves the king in the centre a move longer and gives up the immediate central strike.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: with g3
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares to castle before settling the tension on c4 and d5. White keeps more options than with an immediate capture, at the price of leaving Black to choose whether to take on c4 or to keep the pawn on d5.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.cxd.strategy: Resolves the tension at once and leaves the recapturing knight exposed in the centre to the bishop on g2 and to a possible e-pawn push. White gets a freer, open game and a simple plan: build the centre while Black looks for counterplay.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nc3.strategy: Adds a second attacker to d5 and develops, but ignores the pawn on c4: Black can take it, and White must win it back with a queen check or by attacking c4 again, which costs time. Playable, but it hands Black the choice of how the tension ends.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.cxd.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Exchange Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.cxd.strategy: The natural recapture: the knight reaches the centre, covered by the queen. Black gets quick development and an active game, but the knight is attacked by the bishop on g2 and can be driven off by a central pawn push.
Walks into the bishop on g2: the queen steps onto its diagonal, 6.Bxd5 takes it and Black can only recapture with the knight, giving a queen for a bishop.
Castles first, but the pawn on d5 stays with White. 6.e4 holds it: ...Nxd5 loses a piece to exd5, so Black is a pawn down against a broad centre with only development to show for it.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.cxd.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Exchange Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.cxd.strategy: Develops a piece and covers d4 and e5, putting development ahead of space. White can castle next and builds up gradually instead of grabbing a broad pawn centre.

Gains a tempo on the knight and builds a broad pawn centre, the most ambitious reply. The cost is that the centre becomes a target, so White needs good development behind it against Black's pieces and pawn breaks.

Develops the knight and challenges the one on d5. If Black trades, White recaptures with the b-pawn and gets a broad centre, but the queenside pawns are weakened and the c3 pawn becomes a target for ...c5. Playable, nothing more.
Keeps the knight on the board on a square that watches c4 and d5. Black gives White the centre for now and plans to undermine it from the flank and with pieces, trading White's space for targets.
Sidesteps to b4, where it eyes c2 and d3 but threatens nothing: the queen guards c2, and a3 attacks the knight again. Black loses time while White's centre stands unchallenged.
Retreats to the starting square, so the capture on d5 has gained nothing while White's e4 has won a tempo. The e5 push then drives the knight away again and its pawn blocks the g7-bishop's diagonal.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Brings the king to safety before the centre opens and puts the rook on f8. With the king secure Black can handle the tension on c4 and d5 calmly, whichever way White resolves it.

Supports d5 with a pawn, so that a capture there is met by a pawn recapture and the knight stays on f6. Black builds a solid structure and keeps the choice of castling first or taking on c4, at the price of a slower attack on White's centre.

Takes the pawn, but only for a moment: White wins it back with a queen check on a4 or by attacking c4 with a knight. Black gets a simple position without the tension, but also without a clear plan against White's centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Classical Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Castles first and leaves the tension on c4 and d5 to Black. If Black takes on c4, White plays for development and the long diagonal in return for the pawn; otherwise White keeps the full set-up.
Releases the tension and gives White a semi-open c-file against the c7 pawn. Less ambitious than keeping the tension, but easy to play for a small initiative.

Develops with pressure on d5 but leaves c4 to its fate: if Black takes it, White usually regains it by attacking it again with the knight. Playable, but White's king stays in the centre a move longer than after castling.
Recaptures with the knight, which takes the central square, covered by the queen. Black develops easily, but the knight can be driven off by a central pawn push, so the pieces must stay coordinated.

Recaptures with the queen, which is safe here because the knight on f3 blocks the bishop's diagonal. But the knight on c3 hits it with tempo and the queen must run again, so White develops while Black loses time.
Hopes to recapture with the c-pawn, but White takes first: after 7.dxc6 Nxc6 Black is a pawn down with only a little development to show for it. The pawn is better won back with the knight.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Classical Variation, Modern Defence
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, so White has to show that the bishop on g2 and quick development are worth it. Black must decide later whether to hold the extra pawn or hand it back for time.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Classical Variation, Original Defence
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Backs the d5 pawn, so Black can recapture with a pawn after cxd5 and keeps the central structure intact. Solid and sound, but Black gives White the choice of how to release the tension.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.name: Neo-Grünfeld Defence: Classical Variation, Polgar Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 d5 5.Nf3.strategy: Develops with an attack on d4 and keeps the option of taking on c4 for later. Black brings the pieces out first and decides the pawn structure afterwards, at the risk of letting White set the pace.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, where together with the bishop on g2 it controls e4. White prepares a strong pawn centre while staying flexible about where the other knight goes.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nf.strategy: Develops the knight to cover d4 and e5 and prepares to castle. White keeps the choice of where the other knight goes and how to use the centre, and Black has to settle on a set-up without knowing which structure White wants.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.e4.strategy: Builds the broad pawn centre at once, but the pawn blocks the long diagonal of the bishop on g2 and takes away much of its point. The centre becomes a target for Black's pieces and pawn breaks, so White needs good development behind it.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: The standard set-up: the pawn controls e5 and c5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black builds a compact structure with the king's bishop behind it instead of hitting the centre at once.

Challenges the d4 pawn from the flank at once. White can close the centre and gain space, or take on c5 and let Black win the pawn back; either way Black plays for the long diagonal and the queenside.

Attacks d4 with a developing move. White can gain space by pushing the d-pawn, which sends the knight to the rim, but there it pressures c4, the weak point of a fianchetto set-up, and Black gets queenside play.

Completes the kingside development and adds a second guard of e5 and d4, so White can castle next. The position is sound and flexible, and space together with the long diagonal bishop decide the long fight.

Builds a broad pawn centre before the g1-knight is out. White gains space and Nc3 backs it up, but the e4 pawn blocks the bishop on g2, and the centre becomes the target of Black's pieces and pawn breaks.
Prepares the queenside advance with b4, the rook standing behind the pawn. A slow waiting plan that leaves the king's knight and castling for later, so Black can use the time to strike in the centre.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Carlsbad Variation
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: Piles on d4 with a developing move and invites d5, after which the knight can jump to a5 to attack the c4 pawn, the soft spot of this set-up. A combative choice, much sharper than the quiet systems.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Debrecen Defence
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: Puts the knight on the square that backs a later advance of the e-pawn and leaves the c-pawn free. A flexible, slower set-up that challenges White's centre from behind.

1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.name: King's Indian Defence: Fianchetto Variation, Yugoslav Variation, Rare Line
1.c4 Nf6 2.g3 g6 3.Bg2 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Nc.strategy: Attacks d4 with a pawn at once, so White must choose between closing the centre and releasing the tension. Black loosens the queenside but gets quick counterplay against the white centre.
A quiet, solid move that frees the c7 square for the queen but does not touch White's centre directly. White can complete development undisturbed and pick the plan.
